utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May has got a very bad cold. He won't be able to sit today. Therefore, we decided to sit not having the full bench in order to make progress on testimony and also related to -- we're going to apply Rule 15 bis. Why do we do so? Because we're convinced that this is very much in the interests of justice that we should sit. In there is a no objection from either party, we do suggest that we could sit based on Rule 15 bis, which provides that the other two Judges of the bench, if they believe that this is in the interests of justice, be allowed to sit. Do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Therefore, we're going to call the next witness. I was told that there may be a request from Mr. Naumovski for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honours. Could we just go into private session just for a couple of minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DF, we can move on. When you left the hell of war, if I may put it that way, and came to Busovaca, it was a relief for you because in Busovaca it was a different way of life. It was relatively normal, you could say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no war there yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all that you left formally in your own town you could find here. That is, there was food and electricity and water and all the like, in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, your family, the four of you, were just a few individuals in a huge wave of refugees who arrived in October 1992 from Jajce and that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Busovaca. Could you tell me in your estimate how many refugees arrived from Jajce then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that some 15.000 left Jajce, and some 10.000 of them stayed in Busovaca. Others went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, of that number, of that total number of refugees who arrived in Central Bosnia from Jajce, Kotor Varos and so on, what was the percentage of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have prepared an exhibit, namely this is part of the job of this witness. These are the records -- this is the record of refugees who arrived in Busovaca and who are registered with the local branch of the Red Cross. This is a list, but the witness will explain it. It's not my place to comment on it. We have already given it to the Registry. It looks quite bulky, but the information contained in it is simple and I believe it will save time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D234/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even though this exhibit has several sections, it is one document, so we do not need more numbers than one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DF, we shall not be going through this, but just in principle, whose names are in this list before you? Are these the rosters that were drawn up by the municipal Red Cross in Busovaca, and could you tell us what categories of refugees were included in these registers and which were not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We registered all those who came to register with the Red Cross in Busovaca, and those who came had to register so that we could put them on the list and so that they would be entitled to humanitarian aid. So here, you have the ordinal number, the full name, date of birth, the place that the refugees arrived from, occupation, ethnic origin, where they had been accommodated. So these the are the -- this is the information that we had in these lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, these records are not comprehensive and they do not cover all the refugees who arrived in Busovaca during the war because there were very large categories of displaced persons who are not included there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite right. These records do not include lists of displaced persons from the municipality of Busovaca who came after people from Jajce, Kotor Varos, that is, from the area of Kacuni. We did not know how to register them because we thought it would last only a short period of time, and I would go home in no time at all. So when they came to the Red Cross, we would issue them cards for the humanitarian relief. They were called -- they contained the name of the family provider and the number of members of the family, and the area they had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, excuse me, these ex-police, the expelled persons from the territory of the municipality are not included in these records.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Which other categories are not included here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These records also do not contain, not in full, they do have some, but not most of Travnik people who began to arrive in Busovaca in June 1993 and people from Zenica, because on a couple of occasions, they arrived and we kept a separate record of them, simply to manage better the distribution of the humanitarian relief. Because if somebody said that he'd arrived from Travnik, then it was easier for us to find his card for humanitarian relief, because, of course, everything we did, we did manually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in your assessment during the distribution of humanitarian relief and so on and so forth, how many refugees arrived from the area of the Travnik municipality in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe there were over 2.500.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean who arrived in the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And will you please tell us something about the number of people from Zenica who arrived in large numbers in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After April, I believe there were some 1.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I think we have said enough about the structure of the register you have before you. Can we then conclude that this record, by and large, includes all refugees, until April 1993, who arrived in the municipality of Busovaca, with the exception of those who had been displaced within the municipal territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we then move on to this influx of refugees. In the first wave, were you expelled from that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Jajce, Kotor Varos, and so on, and when did the second big wave arrive in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second big wave was in February 1993, when they arrived from the territory of the municipality of Busovaca, that is, from a locality called Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But when was the next big wave from outside the municipality of Busovaca? You've already said that, but let us try to clarify it, to clarify those stages in which the refugees arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April, also some people were displaced from Putis, Osijek [sic], and also displaced people from Zenica, and then people from Travnik in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, how many thousands of families from Travnik arrived in the territory of the old municipality? You gave us the number a moment ago. Roughly. Yes. You mentioned 2.000 something. Did you mean individuals or families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is reminding me. I think that there is a little mistake in the transcript, page 13, line 13. It is the names of the villages are Putis and Jelinak, not the town of Osijek, which is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the village of Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what you describe now is a general picture of these waves of displaced persons arriving in Busovaca. How did that reflect on the supplies of food and accommodation and generally the quality of life in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult. When there were only people from Jajce, I thought that there was enough food, but the refugees kept coming and food stocks became lower and lower and the situation more and more difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it at all possible to find accommodation after the large wave of people from Travnik, the displaced persons, arrived in Busovaca in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When the displaced people from Jajce arrived in Busovaca, every accommodation was taken, including a lot of weekend homes or vacation homes which were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that there simply wasn't enough room for everyone or with great difficulties people were accommodated, at least those whom you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not enough room. We used all kinds of ways to accommodate people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me also ask you, as a resident of Busovaca in that period, not only a person who worked with the displaced people, did this large influx of refugees also reflect on the quality of overall life in Busovaca? What is your immediate, direct experience of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did. All those who arrived had left their homes, and they all found themselves in a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this large wave of refugees cause the rise in incidents, excesses, and things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that also was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let us try to now wrap up everything we've said so far about the refugees. Can you tell us, on the basis of the information that reached you, how many people from Zenica had left Zenica in that period, and how many people from Travnik left the Travnik region in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what I learned, about 20.000 people from Travnik and 17.000 from Zenica. Of course, not all of them actually stayed in Busovaca, as I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm just asking you about the number of people who were displaced within Central Bosnia. Is that the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to your work, to the job that you did in the Red Cross in Busovaca. When did you join? When did you start working in the local Red Cross in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after the attack on Busovaca in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "the attack on Busovaca." Could you tell the Trial Chamber who attacked Busovaca in late June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the Red Cross at that time was Mr. Stipo Santic. So he gave you a job as an economist so that -- to assist these displaced people with accommodation and distribution of aid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we can move to paragraph 11, which is humanitarian aid distributed in the territory of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of technical points. In addition to the local Red Cross presence, there were several other people working there, people who worked in a warehouse and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your job was such, in fact -- were you able to ever stop working due to shelling and other disruptions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I worked throughout the war and I never -- I was never absent, not a single day. There was one day there was heavy shelling and I was late to work. I arrived only at 12.00 noon because I knew I had to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew that you had to come -- to go there because people were waiting for you, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The humanitarian aid needed to be distributed to people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not only did you go to work despite of the shelling, but also the displaced persons had to go and collect their food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were moments when the shelling -- that there was shelling and there were huge lines in front of the Red Cross offices. The police wanted to chase us away and wanted us to close the office down so that people would not be killed by shells. However, nobody wanted me to stop working, but instead they said, "You just hand it out to us. We don't care whether we're killed by a shell or from hunger." Then I begged them to move across the street into the entry way so that I would -- and that I would do what I needed to do, and then when I would be done I would wave them over, and one of them would come over and take these humanitarian aid and hand it to others as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this preparation of work consisted of what? For each family, you had a separate index card where you entered the data. We will show an example later but this is, in principle, what you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning, who was the only organisation who delivered humanitarian aid to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we received food from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did other humanitarian organisations also contribute?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the -- later UNHCR and other organisations also contributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this humanitarian aid came from different sources. Was it distributed directly to the people who were in need or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took over -- who was taking over the food from the entire region regardless of the source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total humanitarian aid from all humanitarian organisations would be delivered to our central warehouse where we would register it. And then we would distribute this humanitarian aid to some basic point; Merhamet, Dobrotvor, Caritas, so that we would have as few problems as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we've prepared on the basis of the registers that Witness DF has referred, several bundles of evidence but they all boil down to the same. This is a series of certificates, I don't know what name to give them, about the quantities of food delivered to particular areas. The witness just said that at first they distributed the aid through the humanitarian organisations. One was Dobrotvor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Witness DF, Dobrotvor was whose humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Serbian humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Merhamet was a Muslim organisation

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [INTERPRETATION] So the first two exhibits refer to the distribution of humanitarian aid from the municipal Red Cross office in Busovaca to the humanitarian organisations of Dobrotvor, and the Muslim humanitarian organisation Merhamet, and the data are for 1992 and 1993. I must say that we have a problem because there is a host of purely technical data listed here, and they were not translated. It was practically impossible to do so. So I would like to ask the witness to quickly clarify what these documents mean, and if necessary, we can then ask that the full text of it be translated even though it is -- it would be a very a labourious endeavour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait, Mr. Naumovski. Let us try and clarify the situation. Witness DF, if I understand well, you were employed by the local Red Cross; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there were two types of distribution. There was direct distribution to individuals who, as you told us, queued in front of your office, and there was indirect distribution to local humanitarian organisations, as Mr. Naumovski said, Dobrotvor and Merhamet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we distributed the food to the humanitarian organisations, and later, when the Red Cross took over the distribution and did it directly, both for the local residents of Busovaca and for the displaced persons. At first, we didn't even know how to organise ourselves so at first we just were turning over the aid to the Dobrotvor, Merhamet and Caritas organisations. But later on, when it became dangerous and we had no ability to -- for wide-scale distribution, we had distribution points in villages and elsewhere. But after that, we started delivering the aid directly to both the displaced persons and to the local residents of Busovaca. We registered all that on separate index cards which contained a name of the family and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness DF. You have answered my question. So in the beginning, you distributed it through humanitarian organisations, Dobrotvor, Merhamet and Caritas, and these societies, the distribution through these humanitarian organisations, how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of the war. Even in 1975 [sic], some people received aid from the world food programme. These were elderly people, people who lived alone, it was a particular category of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DF, you told us that the distribution could not be done through humanitarian organisations, you mentioned, because it had become too difficult and you then began to distribute relief directly to the population; is that so? When is it that you began to do it directly to the population? As of what date did you begin to distribute aid directly to the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started as early as March, 1993, and when we were -- this is when we were able to deliver the food -- the aid to the humanitarian -- local humanitarian organisation. But as of June, we did it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Mr. Naumovski. I do not know if the witness mentioned 1975. I don't know if this was a slip of the tongue or a misprint or what. Could you please clarify this, but the transcript says 1975.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A mistake. 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the transcript needs to be corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, I would just like to quickly show the witness all of these bundles and ask her to give a very brief comment on each one of those. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this first bundle refers to the humanitarian aid delivered to the Muslim population who lived in Busovaca through 1993. I do not want to take you through all of this, but I put a yellow sticky which I want -- it's on page 7, not counting the cover page. I think we can even mention -- no. Actually, do not say the name of the person. Just tell us what ethnic group the family was, how many members there were, and what is entered here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a Muslim family which arrived in Busovaca from the area of Jajce, had seven family members, received humanitarian aid from the 3rd November, 1992 to 28th August, 1993. The humanitarian aid which they received has been registered by date and also specified what it was; flour, sugar, cooking oil; and the amount received; and also the signature of the person who received it. That is basically it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We just took a random example. If we took any other page, it would be similar information, who the family was, the number of members of the family, the type of aid received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we have the number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski, in relation to this particular page, I take it in number 10, in the first column, means that there are 10 distributions in the period from November 1992 till July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand this? If you look at the entries 1 through 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you give us an idea of what was distributed, let us say in the third -- what falls under number 3 on the 7th of December. What was distributed on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many kilogrammes, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seventy kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later on, what follows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One family packet. How shall I explain that? These were larger-sized packets. We called them family packets, which included oil, cooking oil; beans; sugar; and some canned food; then soy; detergent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is what the family received on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D235/1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry I did not turn on the microphone. Can you take the thinner bundle of documents. This is a register of the supplies that left the main warehouse of the Red Cross and were delivered to the village of Jelinak in February and March. Could you tell us which ethnic group lived in Jelinak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is humanitarian aid which we sent on 14th and 15th of March to the village of Jelinak, and this village was populated by both Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said 14th -- 14th of March and 15th of March, but there is also an entry for February. Could you just say who signed this receipt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zijad Osmancevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Zijad Osmancevic, on 15th March, signed that he received such quantities of humanitarian aid from the organisation. Now, let's try to clarify what Judge Robinson asked you previously. What was delivered on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 15th of March, 450 kilogrammes of flour, 30 litres of cooking oil, 2 1/2 kilogrammes of yeast, 30 kilogrammes of sugar, 50 kilogrammes of beans, and 10 kilogrammes of noodles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. You don't have to read all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, perhaps -- there is no need to go into all the details. I believe we can move on really now we do have a picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that the second page, at the bottom, bears the date of 16 February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a number for this exhibit and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please help us with the other three bundles, and we'll go through them very quickly. It maybe better if each one was numbered separately like we did the first two, so it would be easier to handle all of them. I apologise to the Trial Chamber. We do have a large number of documents all at once, and my apologies to the registrar too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DF, could you please take the document which has "Skradno" and "Loncari" on the cover page. It's -- "Skradno" and "Loncari" should be on the cover page. Can you find that, please? Can you tell the Trial Chamber, what does this bundle refer to? Who lived there and what was distributed there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Witness DF. Could the registrar tell me which is the number given to this document? Is it the document which begins with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the cover page, you will see the names of villages Skradno and Loncari. Do we all have the same document?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year does this refer to and who lived in those villages at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the villages -- in this period, end of 1992 and almost all of 1993, that is, March 1993, May 1993, Skradno and Loncari was populated by Muslims. Excuse me, there were also displaced Muslim people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not only the local residents who were Muslim ethnic background, but also the displaced people who were of Muslim ethnic background. Could you turn to the document where you see registration number 195/93, it is dated 2 May, 1993. And it says that the humanitarian aid was delivered for 103 members. Does that mean that 103 members lived there. And there was a name here, is that Atif Barucija if I can make it out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim? Was he the head of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now just very quickly, how much food was delivered on this second of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 500 kilograms of flour, 55 kilograms of -- litres of oil, 100 kilograms of lentils, 10 kilograms of yeast and also 50 litres detergent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, we will not -- this will end this bundle. We'll have no more questions on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be marked D237/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document, this is, it says Dobrotvor, this is for 1992 and 1993. If you can just say, very briefly, what does this, what do these documents reflect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we delivered humanitarian aid to the Dobrotvor who then delivered food to the population, that is, the refugees of Serbian ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours, I believe there's no need to go any further in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe just to clarify one thing so that there is no confusion. Each document has a separate -- a different title or heading. We did not have the proper forms and so we used the forms which we had so you can see that these have different headings. One is a receipt, one is an invoice and -- but all this refers to the humanitarian aid which was sent out from the central warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D238/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last one which refers to Merhamet. This is, again, 1992, 1993. You already explained to the Trial Chamber. Again, this is documents covering all the food, all the humanitarian aid which were delivered to the Muslim humanitarian organisation, Merhamet, during 1992 and 1993 in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of these documents show that you supplied -- in the Merhamet file, that there is also the locality of Kacuni, isn't it, and this is the first sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the neighbourhood community of Kacuni for Muslim families who lived in the area of Kacuni, that is, to Merhamet. And we supplied Merhamet for other people, for the town and adjacent villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the document on the first page shows that for 481 family members in the neighbourhood community of Kacuni on the 4th of January, 1993 were delivered. It says, 4.3 tonnes of flour, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 106 sacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the total amount was five and a half tonnes of flour. Your Honour, I have no more questions about this matter then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be number D239/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness DF, we were talking about these supplies distribution and so on and so forth, and you have already given the Court a general picture. Perhaps we should merely make it clear to the Court how difficult was life in Busovaca. As of March 1993 until spring of 1994, in the territory of the Busovaca municipality, controlled by the HVO, could one buy something in a shop? Did shops have merchandise which they could sell or was it all based on donations, on aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the first attack on Busovaca happened, all shops closed down and they did not open again, so one could not buy any foodstuffs which means that the whole population, both local and the refugees were turning to the Red Cross for humanitarian relief because even if somebody had money, there was simply nowhere where he could use it to buy something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are an inexhaustible source of the statistical data, so will you please tell us this: In the beginning, when there was a relatively sufficient supply of food and not too many refugees, you would issue a considerable amount of flour per person. However, in 1993, that quantity had to be drastically cut down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the cards that we have attached for humanitarian aid. So that in the beginning, we would issue 10 to 12 kilograms of flour per person, per month, and a litre of edible oil, per person, per month. But in those hard times, and in view of the food shortages, it went down to five kilograms per person and half a litre of edible oil per person, per month, and it wasn't even issued regularly every month. Sometimes some families' turn would come only after a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say somebody's turn would come, does that mean, do I understand you well that you went through the lists as they were, was there any discrimination in the food distribution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no discrimination at all. We simply went down the list. And if we did not have enough relief for all those in need of it, then you can see by the date, we would have it on record, that is, we would distribute the humanitarian relief, as long as we had any. And those who, after we had distributed what we had, then the next group had to wait for the next delivery of relief to us. And then we looked at the dates and then those who received it on the previous occasion were not entitled to it the next occasion so that every month and a half, or two months, everybody would receive his share of the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. So you are telling us that there were no privileged categories or discrimination, that is your experience in the work of the Red Cross. But will you tell the Court if, from the municipal HVO from the municipal authorities, did you ever get any instructions to the contrary? That is that you would have to discriminate individual ethnic groups or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were never issued such instructions. We worked independently. We reported to international humanitarian organisations which brought the humanitarian relief to us and there were never any objections. That is, everybody received the same quantity of the humanitarian relief, be it Croats, Muslims or Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already told the Court that there was a food shortage, there was famine, to put it simply. And you tried all sorts of things to avoid any incidents, even by Croats sometimes when there would be shelling and you would be attempting to give some relief to Muslim refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. There were some moments that were very hard indeed. It was very difficult to work, and I do not really know where did I summon all this energy from and how could I stand it. There were people who threatened me with rifles, but all is well that ends well. I was never really afraid. And when, in that crowd, I would see a Muslim family because, of course, I knew them all very well by that time, both the locals and the refugees, I'd first give a card to them so they could leave that crowd as quickly as possible so as to avoid a possible problem or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Perhaps another question in this regard. What road, from which direction did the humanitarian relief arrive in Busovaca, regardless if it was being sent by the UNHCR or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief logistics for the area of Central Bosnia was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, where the UNHCR had its central warehouse, didn't it? And the Red Cross, they kept their warehouses there for the whole of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the road from Zenica was used to deliver it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But tell us, please, awhile ago you said that the Muslims had attacked Busovaca, that is, the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in January. And what happened in April? Who attacked then? Whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims again, the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you remember, in April 1993, you made an offer to the villagers of the Muslim village of Merdani, near Busovaca, about the delivery of a considerable quantity of food and other relief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember it. I remember we ran into -- we -- there was a problem. They did not receive this humanitarian relief. I don't know why; I was not there. But I know there is a document to that effect. Reportedly there were a number of problems, and there was even gunfire, so that our men with the truck came back to the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is, they did not want to accept that food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they refused to accept that food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, did you have any instructions from military structures or anybody else not to distribute that food? Was there mentioned that there was a preparation of an attack by the HVO or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We did not have anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you consider this evidence to the opposite, if I understand you properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, no comments, Mr. Naumovski. Without comments, and do not lead the witness too much on this matter, please. I believe that the witness has already answered. Besides, she was not there and cannot tell us what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I accept that, Your Honours. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you have already told the Court, in spite of all that shelling, and now we are talking about this really ferocious part of the war as of April 1993 onward, at the time you were doing your job, and I do not really think there is any need to repeat it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is paragraph 17, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps only to say -- to cover only a few questions. Tell us, please, did you, Witness DF -- that is, you worked for the local Red Cross, so you had first-hand information. Did Mr. Dario Kordic have any say in the work of the local Red Cross in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear his views on the distribution of humanitarian aid? Did you ever hear him say some principles which should govern the distribution of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as -- no, and through my boss, Mr. Stipo Santic, Mr. Dario Kordic merely insisted that everybody should receive the same quantities of humanitarian aid regardless of their ethnicity, and insisted on us getting sufficient, adequate quantities of humanitarian aid from international organisations in view of the number of refugees and the local population in the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Naumovski. Witness DF says that Mr. Dario Kordic was committing himself to seeing this distribution equal, but did he have anything to do with the organisation, with the Red Cross organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then why do you say that he was committed, that he undertook, that he did what he could to have it distributed equitably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard him on those occasions when he addressed the population at large.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is just an impression that you gained through a speech of his. You did not really have anything to do with Mr. Dario Kordic in the work of your organisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you just one more question about this. Did you ever, you personally or your boss -- any reports on the food distribution to Mr. Kordic or any information about your work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear -- you told us now -- you told us now about your conclusion about what Mr. Kordic spoke about, the food distribution, when he addressed the population of Busovaca and broader area, but have you ever heard him uphold some other principles, discrimination in the distribution, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps my last question to the witness: In this case, there's been mention about the convoy, a relatively large convoy of humanitarian relief which was allegedly on the -- in the territory of Busovaca on the 28th of April, 1993. It was a large convoy of about 40 lorries. Did you ever hear anything about that convoy? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. All I know is that all humanitarian relief arrived in Zenica, and from Zenica, according to the international organisation's criteria, it was distributed among the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DF.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with that very last question before I turn back to the beginning, if evidence has been given by various members of the international community that a convoy was detained on the 28th of April and then, in due course, released, you're not suggesting that that evidence is wrong, it's just that you weren't in the position of the municipality to see it; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never even heard about that convoy or that it was stopped ever, let alone been on that spot. I was in the office all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, madam, if things were happening involving senior political or military personnel, are you suggesting that in your position as a Red Cross worker you'd get to know about all such matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. And about that one, I never even heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the beginning and to Jajce. When did you yourself leave Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 30th of October at 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard a lot about Jajce and about the fighting there. You've now returned to it, and I think that there are memorials or there's a memorial in Jajce to the number of people involved in the battles, but help us. When people left Jajce in large numbers, it wasn't a bloodbath, was it? There weren't a lot of deaths happening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As people left, it was very hard. Jajce was being shelled. Jajce was shelled between Sunday to Wednesday, day and night, round the clock. I can tell you only this: that for at least that, all sorts of bombs were thrown from aircraft on at least six or eight occasions. So it was very bad. At times they would stop shelling for an hour or two, but right before we left Jajce, I'm telling you they simply never stopped shelling Jajce. One simply could not stand it any more. I spent four months in the cellar with my children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you say specifically whether there were a lot of deaths? That was the specific question asked of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know. I know that in our convoy, as we were leaving, a shell hit a truck. How many died on that occasion, I don't know. But there were dead, even as we were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There were no concentration camps at Jajce, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the picture we have, it's not necessarily important for us, but we have a slight picture and we want a slightly better one, the picture is of the population, at the time that you left, fleeing Jajce en masse and some of it going to, for example, Busovaca. That's the correct picture, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your position in Jajce, you could have no knowledge of what, if any, decisions were being made by the senior military men or by the senior political men or women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Therefore, you have no knowledge of whether there was any arrangement between any of the parties before everyone fled from Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think there was any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you're a Serb. Why did you leave? Could you not have stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not, because my husband is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, therefore, you were, from an early stage, and quite understandably, committed, to an extent, to the Croat cause?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't really put it that way. I was a human being and a just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your husband, what did he do when you got to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He joined the Croatian army and, needless to say, defended us from the attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which brigade was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikola Subic-Zrinjski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You gave us some figures, a lot of figures, and I only want to ask you about two of them. You spoke of some 15.000 people, and then you spoke of some 10.000 people in Busovaca. Can you just tell me what was the 15.000 a figure for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 15.000 was in my estimate the total number of people who left Jajce. And some 10.000 of them stayed in the territory of Busovaca, and 5.000 went on. They simply did not stop. They went to Livno and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only ask you that, madam, because in your summary I understand you to have prepared and signed, you initially said in paragraph seven that there were 10.000 refugees who fled from Jajce and who arrived in Busovaca. Are you now saying there were 15.000 or is 15.000 a different figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a different figure. But by those 10.000, I meant those people who stayed in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the problem because your next sentence in the same paragraph, you said, "Out of 10.000 Jajce refugees, about 5.000 stayed in the part of Busovaca, predominantly populated by Croats." It really doesn't matter very much, but if you'd like to tell us which one of those figures is the one you prefer, and then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about 5.000 stayed in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what's clear from the answers you've given is that, of course, these are very much estimates, aren't they? They're not backed by documentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is documentation. There is documents for those who stayed in Busovaca. The rest, yes, are merely estimates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this morning you had a lot of documents, and I can't pretend to understand them and I hope to deal with them very briefly. You just tell me or rather tell the Judges and I'll hear, what do you say those documents show that's significant? Because if I accept that, then I won't have to look at them again. What do these documents show? They show that you were distributing aid, don't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they show to some extent how you distributed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And probably if we looked at them in detail, and took some examples, they might show that there was less food available as time passed than there was at the beginning. That would be right, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do these documents show anything else? Do they show anything about distribution to Muslims or distribution to Serbs or anything like that or do they just simply show, yes, that the Red Cross distributed aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They show that the Red Cross distributed aid to everybody on an equal basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll come to that, if it's convenient, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall now make a break until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Aid came to your local Red Cross office via the International Committee of the Red Cross, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was distributed either by different organisations, the Croat, the Serb and the Muslim organisations that you had said or it was distributed direct from the premises by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did not go on trucks or lorries or whatever distributing the aid yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you can't speak of how the aid was actually delivered except when it went out of the shop or the building where you were working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received feedback, information from people who had delivered it to those people who were in need of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. But in any event, as paragraph 18 of your summary reveals, you were only distributing aid in the territory of Busovaca that was controlled by the HVO. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because the Mahalla area, whatever else it might have been called, was controlled by the ABiH and you didn't have access to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the Mahalla in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what's the proper name for the Muslim area of Busovaca? I picked it up as being called Mahalla, but can you help me with what the Muslim part of Busovaca is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Merhamet was the Muslim charity organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the area of Busovaca in which the Muslims were living, such as there were, what was that called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims lived both in the town and in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's your statement, you see. It is your statement, isn't it? When did you prepare this summary that we've been supplied with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived here around the 20th or 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because it's your statement and you've signed it, you said, you've spoken of the bit of territory that was controlled by the HVO in Busovaca and then you said, "The ABiH controlled the other half, and we had no access to it." Is that what -- is that the truth? Is that what the position was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later on when it was divided, we had no access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, just coming back to these documents for a minute, just before I get to that, how many people were working at the local Red Cross? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you first started working there what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware that in 1992, the local president of the Red Cross had been a man called -- I'm so sorry. I'll withdraw that. I come back then to the documents. Working for the Red Cross for some time, you must be aware of the -- or be aware to some extent of the various privileges that the Red Cross enjoys as a result of the Geneva Conventions. Are you aware of those privileges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And do you know why the Red Cross has privileges or why it maintains its privileges? What's the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to help all those who are at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you not aware at all of the fact that the Red Cross claims a special position, and because of its neutrality it's always neutral in relation to what's going on. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which is why documents of the International Committee of the Red Cross aren't produced in court, you see. Now, I just wonder, when these documents were produced, which I still haven't looked at, did you seek anyone's permission before you had them produced to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The documents enclosed here are not those of the International Red Cross but, rather, of the Busovaca Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, but the topics that you're dealing with in those documents are the provision of aid which, as you told me a little earlier, was effectively provided via the International Committee, and, therefore, to that extent it is the work of the International Committee. It didn't occur to you to seek anyone's permission before revealing those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These documents are in the Busovaca Red Cross offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on to something else. There was a village called Katici, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, you would know that that was the collection point for Serbs in the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Katici, I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, there would have been and there no doubt was a place where Serbs collected, particularly when they wanted to leave Busovaca, and you, as a Serb, must be able to help us all. I hope you will be able to help us with where it was and what happened. Can you remember what happened to Serbs who wanted to leave the Busovaca area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who wanted to, could leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But do you remember that money was required for their safe passage? Alternatively, they had to sign over their goods as the price of getting permits to leave Busovaca. Do you remember that? Your fellow Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll move on to another topic and cover the few remaining topics quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to move on to another topic, madam, and cover the remaining topics quickly. You knew about Kaonik, the prison camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What Red Cross supplies were sent to Kaonik, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very small, negligible amounts. At the request of the Kaonik warden, we gave certain amounts of aid. Usually it was cooking oil and beans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it was what, starvation rations? Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I just know that part of that humanitarian aid -- when we received a request from the administration after they ran out of their own supplies of food, we then stepped in to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That isn't covered in any of these documents that you've provided us today, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we were to have brought everything, it would have been a lot of documents. There are a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The village of Merdani, which you told the Judges declined aid for a time in 1993, is a Muslim village; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They only declined it once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but they declined it. It's a Muslim village, and the reason they declined it was because they weren't prepared to accept aid from the HVO. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what their reasons were, but they just did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it the HVO that was physically in charge of distributing aid to Merdani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In April 1993, the neighbouring municipality of Kiseljak, still within the same Central Bosnia area, imposed a rule, didn't it, that all distribution of aid should be by the local Red Cross and only by the local Red Cross? Now, you must have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, in your area, all distribution was by the local Red Cross, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in April of 1993 -- just think back please and help us if you will -- you were subject to pressure, the local Red Cross, from the International Committee of the Red Cross to distribute aid to the Muslims, and it was made clear to you that aid would be suspended if you didn't do so. Now, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I know that we gave aid to the Muslims just as we did to the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's break my question into two parts. You were there, and you've had access to the records. You recall an occasion when there was the threat of a suspension of aid, and I'm going to suggest to you that that was in April of 1993. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May it be because it would only be people further up the management chain who would know these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We turn to Skradno, that was an HVO-controlled village and by May, would you accept this, there were only some 22 detained persons remaining there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, help me with this, this would be from what you heard, the correct picture. When refugees arrived in Busovaca, they were regularly enough accommodated in the houses of people who had already left, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With or without the consent of the person whose house it actually was, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Busovaca, a lot of these owners were not present. There were a lot of vacation homes and their owners were in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be, but I move on. By May of 1993, particularly, for example, in Skradno, the empty homes that could have been available to displaced Muslim persons were being guarded by the HVO, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe the same was happening elsewhere, and I'm going to suggest to you, as somebody who was present locally, that the affect of this, depriving refugees of empty homes was to force them, for example, to go to Zenica. It was part of ethnic cleansing. Do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember such things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Stipo Santic, your boss, you saw a lot of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we worked together every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fair enough. He, of course, was on the joint Busovaca commission, wasn't he? You will remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What kind of commission are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the local commission for Busovaca, and I can show you a document if you want to see it but I'll just read you out the members. It was Mr. Santic, Mr. Maric, the mayor, Mr. Morsink, one of the monitors, I think somebody called Beatrice from ICRC, and the other members include Florijan Glavocevic and Zoran Mravak. Do you remember his being a member of this commission along with Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never did see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see if your boss had much to do, Stipo Santic, with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I believe he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we just have a look at one new exhibit, 1197.2. Because you, as a long-term worker of the Red Cross, would presumably discuss with people in your office what was going on in the area generally; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very much. I worked very hard, and I did not have time to chat a lot. I worked from morning until the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, madam, I'm afraid we don't have a version of this in your language. What we we'll do is we'll put it on the ELMO, and I'll read a passage. It says, "A Report of the International Monitors to the 8th of September 1993." And if we look at the third sheet, we can see what appears to be the opinions or the knowledge of the president of the local Red Cross which is why I want your help, please. Third sheet begins with Stipo Santic. You see the local monitors, having spoken to your boss, and I'll read it out slowly, say this, "Stipo Santic, president of the Croat Red Cross (in Busovaca) recognised, for example, that ethnic cleansing has been taking place between Zenica and Busovaca in the past ten days. But he claimed that this cleansing was inevitable, and would continue. Busovaca HVO police officials confirmed this and suggested even that the exchanges should be coordinated at a higher level, and made official, for example, by the international community. BiH officials still strongly condemn officially such a policy, but the pressure of the displaced persons before winter and the death of the--" and the following sentence may not make much sense to you madam as it doesn't necessarily make sense to me, " -- and the death of the ethnic cleansing reversal principle in Geneva, as some financial interests sometimes, makes them slowly have a more pragmatic view on this." So forget that sentence. And then they make this observation to the international observers or monitors, they say, "The HVO Busovaca policy is the official position put forward by Mr. Anto Valenta, vice-president of HVO Herceg-Bosna, who has accompanied Mr. Boban in the last negotiations in Geneva. Mr. Valenta has written a book on this two years ago and, located in Travnik, now in Vitez where he is the most powerful man with Mr. Kordic, he has taken all possible occasions to put his ideas in practice." Now, two points, one related quite specifically to what you were doing. Was what your boss said there about ethnic cleansing discussed in your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I did not perceive it that way either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, you, as the person dealing with the actual distribution of the aid or one of the people will have been able to detect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say I was one of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But you will have been able to detect changes in the proportion of goods going to Muslims or going to Croats. And throughout 1993, would this be right, the amount of aid going to Muslims declined dramatically because the number of Muslims left in Busovaca, itself, declined dramatically. That would be correct, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Ones were leaving others were coming so it's very difficult to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By 1994, there were just a couple of handfuls of Muslims left in Busovaca, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the rest had been driven out, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that they were driven out, and I don't know in what ways they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a war. There was a war, and it was hard. Also, the Croats who had left their own homes were also angry. All kinds of things were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You revealed the truth to us, madam, when you told us that if you saw a Muslim in a queue, you processed him quickly. And the reason you processed him quickly, because if you didn't do that, he would suffer at the hands of the Croats, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if they would suffer, but the situation was very difficult, and I wished to prevent potential conflicts. There was a war, and the Muslims were receiving the same amount of food as Croats. Of course there was anger between or among people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to deal with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to ask the following of this witness: Based on what you told us, madam, that is that Muslims were worried when they would come to your office, they were afraid of possibly hostile reactions from the Croats, well, were the Muslims not talked out of trying to come in to your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was just very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have statistics based on ethnic groups to say exactly what was the amount of distributed aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We kept records on the numbers, the total numbers of both the local population and the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't remember them? Do you have them in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just connected to that, of course, of the Muslims coming to the area -- the figures are only estimates -- a large number were just passing through and then they moved on, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a large number of them stayed until June, some even until August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then they moved on because they were no longer wanted. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know if they were not wanted. Perhaps they were afraid. Perhaps they felt unsafe. I mean, once they've left their home -- once people leave their homes, I don't think they really care about where they will stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course, you must have seen in the town people being arrested and taken off to Kaonik and things like that. Didn't you see that happen from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw anything like that. I would come to work, to the office in the morning, and after that I never went out. The only route -- the only times I went out were to go to the warehouse and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to ask this witness about what she says about the January attack or the April attack. Our position is entirely contrary to her evidence, but I don't think it's necessary for me to explore all matters with her. I'll just ask her one question about the April attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say then, madam, please, in relation to the April attacks, happened at Ahmici? What were you told about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know a thing. I heard that there had been an attack, but I do not know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not very far away, Ahmici, is it? How many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. About ten kilometres. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Witness DF, a couple of matters were raised here and I should like to go through them quickly. Towards the end, His Honour Judge Bennouna asked you when Muslims would come to see you, that is Muslim refugees to get food, that perhaps some incident might take place between the Croats waiting for the food relief and the Muslims waiting in the same queues. Will you tell us, who shelled Busovaca at the time when you were giving out the food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So couldn't that be a reason for some kind of intolerance, if I understood you properly, between the Croats waiting for their food and the Muslims waiting for the food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Document Z1109.2 [sic] was now introduced, and I'll just ask you a question about this. Do you know anything or do you have any knowledge that about that time, September 1993, that is, August 1993, that that was a time of private exchanges, as some people called it, that there were some private exchanges between Busovaca Muslims and Zenica Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps that was so, but I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You don't know if anybody had -- if there were any charges of that kind, who did that, or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not ask any other questions about that. I will ask about the second page of this document 1197.2. Paragraph 3, it says: "Soft Ethnic Cleansing." That is the title of the paragraph, and it is attributed to criminal organisations. I'm drawing your attention to it because the witness surely does not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And I have a few short questions to ask you. Your boss, the president of the local Red Cross, did he ever mention any contacts that he perhaps had with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: My second question: The village of Skradno, I didn't remember the number of persons mentioned by the Prosecutor when he spoke about that village. Twenty-two or something like that. However, this document D237/1, which you explained to us today, on the first page there is a receipt and it says: "Skradno for 103 members, the 2nd of August, 1993." Could that be the approximate number of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it must have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also a question about Kiseljak, but the Court already knows, and I suppose you also know. Did you have any communication with Kiseljak after the January conflict of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. A question about Kaonik. Did the local Red Cross regularly provide Kaonik with food or was it done only as an exception, at the request of the prison administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only when so requested by the prison administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about the departure or transit of a large number of Serbs from Zenica through Busovaca to territories controlled by the army of Bosnian Serbs. When you arrived in Busovaca towards the end of October 1992, did you already see any of such residents or had it happened before you arrived in the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it until I began to work, and I didn't really move around very much before I started to work, and I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. We shall have the opportunity to ask that -- to ask other witnesses about that. The Prosecutor also suggested it was only the International Red Cross which supplied the international relief, but that is not true according to you. Who provided you with food and other relief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the International Red Cross, it was the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Were there also some donations by Caritas or perhaps some private charity or other ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were also -- there was also Caritas and other organisations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So a very broad circle of charity organisations and institutions which were helping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there must have been five or six of them who provided food regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: You told the Court that you were not personally involved in distributing food, on the ground I mean. But there was a document here which said that in early January 1993, a certain quantity of food was sent to the neighbourhood community of Kacuni, and the person who distributed that food on the spot, did he or she have to document it to show who got how much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, whenever it was possible to do so, yes, a report was submitted to the local Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: No, I meant you. Did they have to justify it before you. You, for instance, did some food, go to Kacuni. Did a document had to be submitted to you to show that the food had been distributed to whom, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as a rule, but it wasn't always done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but you had to -- that is for your records, you had to have these so-called input and output and it had to tally so you had to insist on that kind of documentation, didn't you, on certificates or receipts or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would say that we have sent something to somebody, it meant to us that it had reached the intended beneficiary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Very well. And now I am going back to the question you were asked at the beginning of the cross-examination. I didn't ask you anything about that because I didn't see any need for that. And it has to do with Jajce, but you were asked about this by the Prosecution, then I should also like to ask you two or three questions about it.
