Tell me, please, while you were in Jajce, was your -- did your husband go defend against the army of Bosnian Serbs together with the rest of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: In this case, it is alleged that an agreement had -- that an understanding had been reached between the HVO and the army of Bosnian Serbs to surrender Jajce. Your husband was on the front line so you must have heard, you must have received information from your husband. Why did you retreat from Jajce, was it a military defeat or was it surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I know, I think it was a military defeat because my husband, as I said, left the front on the 30th of October at 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: And this will be my last question: Have you ever heard this story, was there any suspicion about the fate of Jajce, about the surrender of Jajce with thousands of your countrymen or rather citizens of Jajce were in touch with them? Have you ever heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions on redirect, Your Honours. Thank you, Witness DF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DF, you have just completed your testimony. We thank you for coming to testify at the Tribunal. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I raise just a couple of matters before Mr. Sayers, it seems, calls the next witness? The first relates to the last witness and her records. I was concerned, of course, not to try and keep out of evidence evidence that the Defence wanted to call on the basis of somebody else's interest, so I didn't object to the evidence. And indeed it's only during the break that I've been able to make further inquiries based on what the witness has told us. And I've been able to speak to counsel who appeared for the International Committee of Red Cross in its action against the Tribunal in relation to the relation to the Bosanski Samac case. It seems possible, to put it no higher than there, that because the work of the witness, in part or whole, on her evidence, in whole, but in mind, in part or whole, would be within the mandate of the International Committee. And indeed because local offices are referred to specifically in their -- I think it's their legislation or in their protocols, they might have had an interest in either objecting to her evidence or objecting to the documents that have been produced. We now know that she had made no request of them. The matter hadn't been clarified. The Chamber will have observed, from the questions I asked before the break, that there may be very little need ever to turn to these exhibits again, because I think they were summarised in a few questions and answers, although Mr. Naumovski drew some comfort from a couple of documents in re-examination. And I draw all this to the Court's attention. If it took the view that there was absolutely no value in these documents or no value beyond what it's already heard and was concerned not to cause offence to an important party in all these historical matters, one way to deal with it might be to no longer count the exhibits as produced, but it's entirely a matter for the Court. And I have -- after this has been disposed of, there is one short administrative matter that I'd like to deal with before we call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Naumovski, please be brief, because I do not believe that this should give rise to a major debate. I do not quite understand why Mr. Nice came back to this, but it is so. We've discussed this earlier on. We're dealing with a witness, very local witness, who apparently did not have any access to major decisions made by the Red Cross. All the documents we have received had to do with the way food was distributed and do not, at all, violate the major principles of the Red Cross i.e., independence and neutrality among others. Therefore we shouldn't be dragged into unnecessary discussion. So it's up to you, Mr. Naumovski, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you said what I was about to say. That was precisely that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should the Red Cross wish to intervene in some way or other, it will do so. But for the time being, we have decided to listen to this witness. We have listened to her starting from the idea, also from the fact, that she was a local employee, a locally-recruited employee dealing with -- carrying out things and not making decisions. She was distributing food at the local level and that is about it. Do you have any further questions, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On another issue maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only on another issue which will only take a minute. We are not sitting tomorrow and we're not sitting on Monday and, of course, Judge May isn't with us today. Several affidavits have been introduced this week and in order to avoid offending the seven day rule, I had it in mind that we might carve out of the timetable ten minutes at the end of today and then dispose of this week's affidavits, and in that orderly way save time and ensure that nothing got overlooked. I suspect that you're not necessarily in a position to make decisions about affidavits if you're not fully formed with three judges. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what we're going to do: We're going to deal with the next testimony and fending objections by the Defence, we shall work a little -- we shall postpone the time period scheduled or catered for the affidavits, so you'll have time until Tuesday. If the Defence agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. Under the circumstances, and just for the Trial Chamber's information, we have prepared a document that summarises all the affidavits filed to date, at least the ones that have not already been previously summarised, as we were requested to do, and I can distribute that to the Trial Chamber at the end of the evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I think it would be very useful. Thank you. Can we call the next witness? Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course we can call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the issue of the affidavits is now postponed, so you've got more time. You've got time until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll discuss that on Tuesday. Can we call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's an application for protective measures. If we could go into private session, I can explain it in a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. The Court has granted the request for protective measures that you requested, and you will be known, for purposes of this examination, as Witness DG. I would like you just to read the name that is contained on this piece of paper, please, and confirm for the Judges that this is indeed your name, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it would be possible to go into private session while we go over the basic identifying background data regarding the witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In 1993, the work of the police force was extremely difficult. The conditions were very bad in 1993. There was an open conflict, there was a war, and it was a fierce war that went on. And one of tasks of the police was to protect the defence lines and prevent the Muslim forces from crossing them. We only had four or five police officers for civilian duties and we tried to cover the territory of the Busovaca municipality and tried to provide a minimum of security for the civilian population living there. In addition to those problems, I need to mention that the lack of vehicles, fuel, equipment, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's take it one step at a time, Witness DG. The Court has heard considerable evidence about the influx of refugees, undocumented refugees, into the Busovaca municipality at various times throughout 1993. There's no need to repeat all of that. Just from the perspective of the law enforcement officer, sir, could you give the Judges some sort of -- some kind of picture as to the impact that this influx of refugees had on law and order in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: As far as this problem is concerned, that was one of the most acute problems. Because in 1993, the number of displaced and refugees approached the number of the local population, the police has -- had no accurate registration of these individuals. We did not know whether some of them had criminal records, so it was extremely hard for us to cover that, and if any crime occurred, we were unable to respond because we did not have the right information, data on the people who were there. We did not have their files and so on. And in such conditions, I believe it was very, very hard to work and I need to point out that these displaced people and refugees were expelled by mostly Muslims and Serbs, and it made things much more difficult for the local population in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1993, could you tell the Court about how many officers the police precinct actually had in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In early 1993, combined active duty and reserve police officers, the number was around 70. I'm not exactly sure, but as the year went on, the police force kept diminishing. Some of them were killed in the front lines, some of them were manning the defence lines, and we needed to send a number of police officers to the lines of defence in the various shifts. So by the end of 1993, the number of police officers was about 35. They were divided into two groups of 15 each. That is, they went to the lines of defence in cases of any attacks or any combat operations of any significant scale, and they stayed there for as long as it was necessary, whereas the other five or six police officers stayed behind and worked on regular activities which included distribution of humanitarian aid, on-site investigations of various crimes and so on. Everything else that is part and parcel of the police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And in terms of the equipment that you had; cars and so forth, to be able to patrol the municipality, could you just give the Trial Chamber a sense of how well equipped your police force was, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: There was a problem with the fuel. If you had vehicles, then the problems were how to use those vehicles. We had to use them to drive the police officers to the lines of defence, so as far as the overall work of the police force is concerned, the conditions were very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you able to pay your men, sir, when you were (redacted) in September of 1993 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In 1993, I don't believe we paid out any salaries, only in 1994, after the truce was signed by -- in 1993, there were no salaries paid out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: During the civil war in your municipality, sir, what would you assess as being the most significant duty or obligation facing the civilian police force at least from your perspective (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: First of all, the first task of the police force was defence of the lines of defence because if that collapsed, then everything else would collapse. There were other duties relating to the security of citizens, so that involved patrolling the territory of Busovaca municipality, and we tried to keep the level of security at the highest level. Also, there was investigation of all criminal acts that occurred there so that the regular life could continue. And there were all kinds of problems. There were altercations and quarrels between the displaced and refugees on the one side, and the local people on the other, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In terms of the military balance of power, if you have any basis to give us your estimate, sir, how would you assess the armed forces of the ABiH as compared to the armed forces of the HVO in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: The ratio was at least one to ten. The mobilisation, the mobilisation was carried out at 110 per cent level. That means that every -- all male potential conscripts were mobilised. And as far as that period is concerned, everything was under control and all criminal acts were also under the jurisdiction of military police because all people had -- were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In terms of the one to ten estimate that you gave us, in whose favour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In favour of the Muslims, of course. We were -- there were -- the Croats were ten times fewer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the military police. Were the civilian police and the military police working side by side during this time or did the civilian police essentially cease to function and their function was taken over by the military police or not. You tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Sometime in 1992, towards the end of 1992, the military police took over the police station, the public security station in Busovaca, and at that time, the civilian police ceased to exist. But in late 1992, early 1993, the military police withdrew from the police station, the public security station, and then the civilian police was -- again re-established and started to work. They did their work because at that time, they were all active military personnel and they were -- they had much more work but we continued to do our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If a crime were to be committed involving a soldier, whose jurisdiction would that fall under? Did the civilian police have any jurisdiction to investigate or take any punitive measures against the responsible person or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Because everyone was mobilised, the civilian police had no jurisdiction. Everything became the jurisdiction of the military police. But we would both go on the scenes of crime to do our work during 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What kinds of things fell within the jurisdiction of the civilian police then, Witness DG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: As far as the jurisdiction of the civilian police, it was the defence of the territory. This was the principal task. For the rest, it was the investigation of certain crimes that were not that serious, and trying to resolve all problems that had arisen, let's say between the refugees and displaced persons and the local population, and all other problems that were topical at the time, such as distribution of humanitarian aid under the threat of shelling and other work that falls within the police work. We also had to do certain things that would fall within the inspection domain, but we had to do whatever we could in order to make the life as tolerable as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Two points. With respect to the shelling that you mentioned, was Busovaca shelled? If it was, how frequently and by whom, sir, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Busovaca was shelled frequently by the Muslims. Those shells fell around the town and there were cases when the civilians were killed. I believe that in 1993, the shelling was especially intense. I think most of all in April and middle part of the year. We had an officer who was trained in demining, and he did that especially to provide additional safety for the children in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Second point, checkpoints. Did the civilian police have any duties or responsibilities in connection with checkpoints, about which we've heard a lot of evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian police had two checkpoints. One was near the restaurant Sunce on the road leading from Busovaca to Kaonik, and the other was at the Mediapan company which was on the road to Zenica. There were police officers whose task was to control the movement of people and goods and everything else. So their tasks were clearly defined. I believe that at one of these checkpoints, at the restaurant Sunce, there was also the military police presence so that he could solve problems that would fall within his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was the president of the municipal HVO government (redacted) (redacted), Witness DG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Zoran Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you report to him in discussing the security situation regarding -- or throughout Busovaca municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: We sent reports to Mr. Maric. I did so. It was done on a regular basis. Every other day we would compile a report on everything that happened during that period, and occasionally we would try to talk to him, and we would try to solve the problems as much as it was possible, even though both of us were not really able to solve everything because it was a time of war and it was difficult to operate. Also, we sent reports to the brigade commanders so that he could take steps within his jurisdiction; that is, if we registered anything that members of his brigade may have done, we reported that to him so that he could take certain steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the brigade commander you just mentioned, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Dusko Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. The next thing I'd like to cover with you, Witness DG, is events leading up to the ABiH attack in Busovaca in the latter part of January 1993. Could you just give the Trial Chamber a feel for the events that immediately preceded that attack, as you saw them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Before the attack of ABiH, there were certain things that foreshadowed an inevitable conflict. There was a series of incidents throughout the territory. There was a concentration of forces at Kacuni. It was widely known that the 7th Muslim Brigade was stationed there and that other Bosniak troops were being deployed there. The women and children were moving out while the men stayed behind in the town. Everything -- it was clear that some problems were coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you hear about an incident involving a checkpoint, and people being apprehended at that checkpoint, a few days before the fighting in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I heard about it. People talked about it on those days. I heard that at a checkpoint manned by Bosnian Muslims, Ignjac Kostroman had been stopped and there were problems there, but some humanitarian aid was passing through and also some men arrived from Busovaca, and the situation was resolved to everybody's satisfaction, if I can put it that way. But I heard that he was moving from Travnik and Busovaca in the direction of Kresevo, and later it was talked about a lot, even on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anybody make the contention that Mr. Kordic was present at this incident in which Mr. Kostroman was apprehended by ABiH troops at that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I did not hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me draw your attention to an incident on January the 24th of 1993, just one day before the outbreak of fighting, sir. Did you hear about any provocations or incidents at the checkpoint in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I heard that on that date, 24th, I think it was a Sunday, at the checkpoint in Kacuni two Croats were killed. This incident happened -- I don't know the reasons, but the Muslims had erected a checkpoint and they killed two Croats. Of course, this had an echo and it affected the security situation. People saw that an open conflict was imminent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of those two Croats who were killed at the checkpoint on the 24th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: One was from Busovaca, Ivica Petrovic. He was a military police. I knew him. And the other one, I believe, was either from Kresevo or Kiseljak. His first name was Igor. I don't know his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what you were -- what your involvement in the fighting on the 25th of January was, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: On the 25th, I was at Krcevine. That was the headquarters of the 2nd Battalion. I reported there to see what was going on and to see what my role in it would be, because I saw that on the 25th, the open conflict had broken out and in those -- at that day, I spent there, and in the evening, we -- the evening we spent in the battalion headquarters. I think we went to the front line at the village of Kula. Myself and several colleagues, we went to see -- because there was already shooting and then we went back to Krcevine to the battalion and we told them that there was -- that there weren't enough soldiers there and that we needed to mobilise more people, that there were huge areas completely empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As I understand it, as you previously testified, you were wounded the next day, January 26th, 1993, and you then went to work for the police -- for the civilian police as an investigator, but were hospitalised again in March of 1993 because of problems with your internal organs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you had to undergo surgery, convalescing at home and you began to resume your responsibilities with the police precinct in the latter part of April, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, sir. Just to address a specific incident that the Prosecution claims occurred in this case. There is a contention made that a large UNHCR convoy escorted by armoured vehicles from UNPROFOR was hijacked in the town of Busovaca on April 28th, 1993. Did you ever hear anything about that or see anything of that sort in Busovaca, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I never heard anything about it, nor did I see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You've mentioned the checkpoints that were maintained by the civilian police force, two in number. Could you tell the Court how the civilian policemen that actually manned those checkpoints were dressed? Were they wearing camouflage uniforms? Were they wearing something else? You tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: The checkpoint usually was manned by two policemen, two civilian policemen, and a military policemen next to the Sunce restaurant where -- there was another place, again, two policemen. At first they wore camouflage uniforms then they were in blue uniforms. As for their work, there was a sequence of tasks which they had to perform and they simply complied with that, so there was nothing out of the ordinary. The chief task was the transportation of merchandise. If something came from Herzegovina, then had he the authority from the government of Herceg-Bosna or somebody else to see what it was. To see whether we agreed with that and let it through. As for the transportation of merchandise within Busovaca, that was being done by the Department of Economy and that was, of course, the task of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right, Witness DG, let me ask you a question about Mr. Kordic. What authority did he have in relation to checkpoints and the manning of checkpoints by the civilian police. Did he have any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No authority in so far as the checkpoints and the -- or the civilian police were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. In all of the time that you were in the police force, throughout the civil war, sir, have you ever heard of any convoys being apprehended in Busovaca or that Mr. Kordic had any role in such an affair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I did not hear that he ever stopped a convoy in Busovaca or that Mr. Kordic had something to do with it. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, moving on to paragraph 22, and we're trying to take this as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, I did not have to submit any reports. From time to time, I would notify about some events which would be of interest, and were of interest to politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did Mr. Kordic ever issue any orders to you or to any of the police officers under your command, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that Mr. Kordic ever issued an order to the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, any officer, any soldier in that brigade, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One final question. You've known Mr. Kordic for some time. Having known him since your student days, have you ever heard him use derogatory or pejorative terms when referring to members of any other ethnic group other than Croats, obviously?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I did not hear anything like that, because he's simply not like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In any of his private or public statements, have you ever heard Mr. Kordic advocate hatred, discrimination or the perpetration of violence against any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I did not hear anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court a little bit about Mr. Kordic as you saw him, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, sorry for interrupting you. I'd like to ask Witness DG the following thing. He just told us that, as a rule, he would not inform Mr. Dario Kordic, but that every now and then he would on issues that would interest or concern him as a politician. Could the witness be more specific? What was the kind of information, Witness DG, that you would send to Dario Kordic and in what capacity would you send him this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I can explain that. As far as I can remember now, I believe I submitted two reports to him (redacted). One concerned problems in the work of the Red Cross, because there had been complaints registered by citizens. They were not happy about it. I believe it was late 1993, end of 1993, something like that. I believe I sent him that kind of information because, naturally, I mean, he was a politician, that he should be concerned about these matters. Also in my capacity as (redacted) (redacted). These were the aggregate indicators about the number of crimes, offences, how the police worked in 1993, what it did, where it did. I mean those were simply aggregate indicators of the crimes. I believe those were the two instances when I informed Mr. Kordic about our activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second part of the question I wanted to put to you, Witness DG, when you would inform him or when you would talk to him, what was the capacity he was in? What was his political responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really know which political office he held at the time. I simply wrote to Mr. Dario Kordic. I never wrote any title or rank or anything, simply Mr. Dario Kordic. I don't really know what he did at the time or what was the office he held. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you would send documents to him such as statistics as to work done by the police. I mean, these are significant documents, after all, and you wouldn't send such documents to just anybody. You selected Dario Kordic for some reason, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes. He was a politician and he was well known. He was the president or the vice-president of the HDZ. I don't know exactly, but I know that he was a politician, and a politician who was highly appreciated in the area. So I submitted information to him because I believed it would be of interest to him. It was very important, the distribution of humanitarian relief, the work of the police, communication with citizens, and we simply thought people might ask him if they were not happy about something, and he needed information to be able to answer. It is the practice to this day that the (redacted) police inform politicians of matters of interest to them, the humanitarian aid, the situation with the traffic, crime rate, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I only have one composite exhibit for Witness DG. This was already admitted as Exhibit D450 in the Blaskic case, Your Honours. If I might just have it distributed and marked as an exhibit in this case. I only have a very few questions for the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit will be marked D240/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You probably can't read the index, Witness DG, but there are a number of self-explanatory items on there. Item A is entitled Crimes Against Muslims; item B, Crimes Against Croats; item C, the mosque, I'll ask you some questions about that in just a minute; item D, Crimes by Muslims; E, The Topalovic Case; F, Statements of Muslims Desiring to Leave Busovaca; G, Statements of Croats Arriving in Busovaca From ABiH Territory; H, Busovaca Civil Police Reports; I and J, Data Regarding Croat Refugees Who Left Portions of Busovaca Municipality Under the Control of the ABiH; and item K, Data About the Destruction of Croat Houses in the Busovaca Municipality. Could you just turn to tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I be heard first, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have no idea what the foundation is for this witness producing this enormous amount of material, and if it is admissible through him, the foundation ought to be laid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice [sic], could you please introduce this document? What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mean "Mr. Sayers," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only tab that I wanted to draw to this witness's attention was tab H.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just take a look at tab H which is part of this Blaskic exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. This is the question I wanted to put to you: You just read out the index of this document, but what is this? Is this a report? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These are a compilation of records maintained in the civilian police department at the time that Witness DG was, a police officer; (redacted) (redacted). So these are official records, and I just wanted to get the witness to review these and just confirm that these were authentic records of the police department, Your Honour. Since there was a foundation objection made, I think that's the appropriate way to address the foundation, (redacted) (redacted), confirm that these are indeed records of the police department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I observe that the majority of the material is untranslated. I obviously can't deal with the exhibit at all. Also to observe that apparently it's only one part of it, which is part H that Mr. Sayers now wants in. What mustn't happen is that a document be let in on some ground as to some tiny part of it, in due course the whole document being referred to for some other purpose. And if there's only a purpose in relation to part H, then at the most part H should go in. But if part H isn't translated, I don't really know how I'm supposed to deal with it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Sayers. If I understood properly, according to you, the foundation you offer is that these are document records from the police department at a time when Witness DG was working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was going to turn your attention specifically to tab H, but I wonder if you could just review these records. Just take a minute or so to review those records, sir, and could you just tell the Trial Chamber whether these are indeed records that were maintained by the civilian police department in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes. These are documents that were written at the police station in Busovaca. These are official notes written by members of the police station about individual incidents, taking of statements, press releases about individual developments in order to draw the attention of the public to them, and we see here statements of citizens about the developments or events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Witness DG, if I can interrupt you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I must say, Your Honours, Mr. Nice does have a point since there appear not to be translations here or at least of some of these documents, which is surprising to me since this is the exhibit, the original exhibit in Blaskic. So I don't propose to ask Witness DG any specific questions about these documents. I don't think that would necessarily be fair to the Prosecution. We'll just have to wait and submit these, as we've done, to the Translation Unit and get translations in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might, though, test your memory, Witness DG.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And for purposes of this series of questions that deals with paragraph 25, I wonder if we might go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Witness DG, we've heard in September of 1993 the mosque in Busovaca was set on fire or caught fire. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether you had any connection with trying to put that fire out or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes, when the mosque in Busovaca was set on fire, I was in the police station with my colleagues. I came out to the scene. We tried to put the fire out, but it was impossible because the fire had already reached the roof and we also called the firemen. They arrived after a while and tried to extinguish the fire. I believe the damage was considerable, but the fire was eventually put out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Just a few final topics and I will be through in five minutes, I hope. There's been a contention in this case that the Bosnian Croats, through their leadership, indulged in a policy of deliberate persecution harassment of people of non-Croat ethnicity. As the chief of police from September of 1939 until the end of the war, could you give the Trial Chamber your perspective on the accuracy or legitimacy of those sort of contentions there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: That contention is absolutely false. We never had any such orders. What happened, happened. And what happened was a large-scale horrible war which victimised us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any instructions or encouragement to turn a blind eye to the bad things that were happening to Muslim and Serb residents of the municipality, Witness DG?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I never received any such orders, nor did anyone tell me to do anything like that. Quite simply, there were no such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you ever ordered to ease up on your attempted investigation of crimes committed against Muslims specifically or to discriminate against them in any other way, or encouraged either directly or indirectly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, never, either directly or indirectly. We were always asked to do our utmost to protect everybody who happened to be in the territory at the time, and to try to ensure a normal life in so far as that was possible at that time and in view of that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. As I understand it, sir, Mr. Franjo Kristo was the commander of the civilian police force during 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He was involved, and the Court's heard a lot of evidence about this. He was involved with a group of other Busovaca residents, including Mr. Kordic, in stopping a JNA convoy transporting weapons, I believe, at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes. Franjo Kristo was the commander of the public security station in 1991, and his immediate superior was Husnija Neslanovic. I heard about the incident in 1991 with the convoy of armament of the JNA was -- took place. Dario participated in that and Franjo, but Husnija Neslanovic did not want to get involved in this, refused to take part. They did not want to get in trouble with the Yugoslav People's Army, and since I know Franjo very well, I know that he had major problems because he stopped that convoy. He had those problems with Husnija Neslanovic and the Muslim police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Kristo after this convoy incident that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, what I heard was that his name was struck off the payroll. That he did not get his salary anymore. That Neslanovic simply could not approve such an action against the Yugoslav People's Army and showed him, without mixed words, that he disapproved of that; so he had problems afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much indeed. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with some topics with this witness, but almost certainly I shan't be able to cover anything, but there's another witness coming from the same municipality next week so I should be able to put most of my case one way or the other. I hope that's satisfactory. Alternatively, to cover matters extensively, would not be possible this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We aren't going to look at these documents that have been produced today. They may or may not be looked at later. But help me with this, please, when these documents were selected for the Blaskic case, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I believe that I was still with the police at the time. I don't know when they were being selected, and I don't know who selected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It follows, therefore, that you don't know by what criteria they have been selected at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: As far as criteria are concerned, I don't know what criteria were used by -- I know that these documents are all from the Busovaca police station, that they were all drafted in the Busovaca police station and that as such, I can say that those are the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I do not think it would really be in order to go back to that discussion of this document because you do not have the translations. You do not know the contents of these documents and, therefore, I do not think it would be in order to waste too much time discussing these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to spend any more time discussing these documents for I've reached the point I want to and it's this: At the time of the selection of these documents, the full records of the police station existed, probably those full records exist to this day. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: The police records, that is the archive, is in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you, yourself, turned to that archive at all before coming here to give evidence today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you try to or did you simply not even think of doing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I simply didn't need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your summary that we were served, whenever it was, how long has that been in the preparation, please; days, weeks, months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I prepared the outline when I arrived here, that is, in the last four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With no earlier discussions with the lawyers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I talked to the lawyers about maybe a year ago in Busovaca on whether I would come here and testify and give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When were you first asked to turn your mind back, please, to the incident at the checkpoint. When did you first start the process of remembering all about the checkpoint incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Can you please specify what incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The one where you told us something about Mr. Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: That was the incident in Kacuni. When we first talked in Busovaca, we talked in general about all topics, and I think one of the topics was this. There was a time line, and what I remembered, what I didn't remember, what happened, what didn't happen, and it is probably at that time that we also covered that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And until then and between 1993 and then, 1999, had you had any occasion to focus on that incident and try and remember details about it or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I didn't think about it, but I remembered it because, in that period, everybody talked about it. You could hear it on the radio and elsewhere. It was very clear to everyone that had the humanitarian aid convoy not appear, he would not be able to get out of there and it wouldn't -- it all would not have ended up well for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come to the humanitarian aid convoy and its involvement in all of this in a minute. But between 1993 and 1999, you hadn't looked at any police report on this incident, had you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have a diary or do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I have nothing specially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So in six years, or after six years and then now after seven, you are able to remember something about Mr. Kostroman. What happened to him, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Excuse me, shall I repeat what happened to him at the checkpoint? I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I want the detail from you, please, of what happened to Mr. Kostroman at that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I know that in those days, people talked and I heard that on that day at the checkpoint in Kacuni, Kostroman was stopped, together with his team. He was going from Travnik in the direction of Kresevo his home, he was stopped by the Muslims, that there were some problems. I heard that a convoy arrived and, meanwhile, some men heard that in Busovaca and went over there to see what was going on. And it -- and I don't know how it ended up. I don't know if they came back to Busovaca, but I know that there were no problems. This is what I remember, this is what I -- what stayed in my memory, but this event echoed around because Mr. Kostroman at that time was a well-known politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he kidnapped and abducted or stopped or what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I cannot specify those details. I heard what I heard. I was not present there, and I heard what I heard. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said something -- this is the last question about the detail I'm going to ask you about because of want of time, but you've said something about -- one last of two questions -- something about Kresevo. Who was going to Kresevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Mr. Kostroman, from what I heard. He was going either from Vitez or Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the last question on detail, before I move on, this humanitarian aid convoy, what part did that play?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: You mean the convoy which appeared at a checkpoint when Mr. Kostroman was stopped?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. What part did that play?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what role it played, but it probably appeared, and this is what created all this commotion and this is why Mr. Kostroman was able to pull out, but I did not hear any further details.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, we know -- what was the date of this incident? Perhaps you'll help us with that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly, but I know that it was before the conflict. Perhaps a couple of days before. I cannot recall exactly, but I -- perhaps a couple of days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I was in Busovaca, in the police -- no, the inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, what I don't quite understand from your summary -- perhaps you can help me with this -- is your paragraph 3 where you say that in the second part of 1992 you joined the HVO as a soldier, you were sent to the front line and defended Paklarevo, and on the 26th of January you were injured. Now, were you continuously at the front line until you were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No. At that time, the members of the Busovaca HVO went to the line of defence at Paklarevo against the army of Bosnian Serbs, and they would stay there three to five days. I went twice. So that means that I spent four or five days the first tour and then went back, did my regular work, and went again. I think I was there for only two or three days. It was a shorter period of next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So are you telling the Judges that on the day that Kostroman was -- whatever happened to him, you were actually in Busovaca that very same day, that very same evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I was somewhere in the town. I don't know exactly where. I cannot recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who brought you the news of this incident involving Kostroman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: People talked around town. That was the top story of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What else happened in town that very evening, please? Anything special?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, for example, if on the same evening the mosque had caught fire, you'd remember that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In those -- in that period, there was a series of incidents. One followed the other. It is hard to remember all of them. It was -- there was just this horrible feeling that the conflict was pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You still can't remember any other particular incident that happened that evening after the incident at the checkpoint? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you repeat this? I'm not quite sure what you were driving at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You really can't remember any other particular event happening on that same evening of the checkpoint event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what I should try to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you obviously can't. It was that evening that the Muslim businesses were blown up. Are you sure you were in Busovaca that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: That evening, I was in Busovaca, at home with my family. And in those days, as I said, there was a series of incidents. Now that you mention that these Muslim premises were blown up; yes, there were explosive devices set up in Muslim business premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In fact, all the Muslim premises were destroyed that evening, weren't they? Small town, only about 11 of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it was all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But there was something that happened that evening as well. Take your time. Tell us what it was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. You mean the killing of -- the murder of Mr. Delija?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I think that that happened around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell us about that. Who murdered him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know who murdered him. I heard that a group arrived in front of Mr. Delija's house and that he was killed at his doorstep. This is what I heard. This is what people talked about in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time, you were a soldier. In a few weeks' time, you would become a policeman and quite a senior policeman. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: At that time, I was a regular soldier. After that, I became a regular police officer. It wasn't a high position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the following year you became chief of police, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Only towards the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, would you confirm if this be right, but correct me if I'm wrong, would this be right: that the International Community, represented by the United Nations soldiers, were relatively regular visitors in and out of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And they did their best to keep contacts with policemen and with soldiers, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I'm not sure they did everything they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would it be your experience -- correct me if I'm wrong -- that all parties, and in particular the Croats and the Muslims, would make complaints of what was troubling them to the soldiers of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: They probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you have described at the checkpoint, which you say was talked about by everyone, was a highly inflammatory act involving one of Bosnia's foremost Croatian politicians, Kostroman; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to. Could you please clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To hold up, whether he was kidnapped, abducted, disarmed, whatever happened to him, to interfere with someone of the importance of Mr. Kostroman would be a highly inflammatory act; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you, incidentally, accept that what followed, the bombings and the murder of Delija were connected to that act or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if they weren't connected, can you think of any good reason why the local Croats wouldn't complain of Kostroman's arrest to the United Nations soldiers? Can you think of any good reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I'm not sure that they did not complain. I don't know whether they did complain, and I'm not sure whether they complained.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know either, but we've only got the material we've got at the moment. Likewise, can you help me with this: If, as you say or as you allow for, the bombings of the Muslim premises and the murder of Delija were in no way connected to the HVO, we should find full and detailed police reports on the incidents, shouldn't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what went on at the time. I was not with the police force at the time, and I said what I heard about what had happened in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness DG, you were very soon to become a policeman, and although we don't know whether they'll be admitted into evidence, you've spoken of records, and I haven't gone through them and I don't know what is contained, but please just think again. If the bombing of Muslim premises and the murder of Delija were in no way connected to the HVO, we should find full and unbiased reports on these events in your records, shouldn't we? Not your records. I mean the local police records.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what's contained in the archives. I did not work with the police at the time, and what I heard I heard being spoken about in town and I said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you know, and it was well known in your side of the community at the time, that these events were all connected and that what happened to Delija was a nasty revenge attack following on an incident at a checkpoint involving Mr. Kordic. That's what you know to be the case, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know that and I do not agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course -- by whom were you appointed to your job in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I think it was the municipal assembly. It was wartime and the police was not well linked up. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kristo was appointed by Kordic and Kostroman, would you accept that? We can show you the document if necessary, but would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I wouldn't accept that and I don't know who appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's Exhibit 175, I'm not going to trouble the Court with the time, and 175.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kristo, incidentally, do you still keep contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, we -- we talk to each other, but infrequently. He doesn't live in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know what troubles he eventually faced in relation to this conflict with the local courts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Excuse me, what conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he named as a defendant in trials related to the conflict, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was not. I have no access to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before you became a member of the police station, were you aware that he was involved in obtaining guns, trading in and obtaining guns and other weapons, maybe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I didn't know. I knew that at the time, everybody was acquiring weapons, both Croats and Muslims because it was clear that a war was coming our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was on good terms with Dario Kordic, wasn't he, Kristo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know what their relations were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me just pursue one other matter. Incidentally, when you say there was an attack on Busovaca in the early part of January -- in January 1993, it's not accepted -- there was fighting, but it's not accepted that it was an attack by the Muslims on Busovaca. Just tell us so we can follow this, where do you say the first fighting was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know where the first fighting broke out. I think this was all -- the whole confrontation started on Monday, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were -- by two days later, you were wounded. Where were you treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I was wounded in my left leg. The bullet ricocheted --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. I meant in which town were you treated, not whereabouts on your body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I was at home, I convalesced at home. I went to the hospital, that is the health centre. I was given first aid. They cleaned out my leg, took out the shrapnel. This was not a direct hit so it was a lighter type of injury, and I went back to my wife and children and I continued to go and then would occasionally go to have my wounds -- my wound dressed in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So you were around and on the streets of Busovaca at all material times, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were around Busovaca and, to a degree, you were on the streets at all material times. At all the times we were talking about in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I couldn't walk around immediately. I was mostly at home, but I could walk a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall, on the 26th and 27th of January, a man, Zoran Glavocevic, instructing Muslims to surrender and to hand over their arms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, can you explain to the Judges how the Muslims found themselves in Kaonik? You were there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I heard that in the first days, there was fighting in town and that a number of Muslims who were -- who were fit for military service were taken to Kaonik. This was the rumour mill in town that I heard in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You subsequently became a policeman with access to the information of the authorities. It was true, wasn't it? The Muslims were rounded up and carted off to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I would not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course policemen of Muslim ethnicity, what happened to them? They weren't allowed to work in the police station, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: That is not correct. I think that there were a couple of Muslim police officers who worked in the Busovaca police station at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was Sliskovic's role in all of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the police in any way under Sliskovic's control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A matter of detail which I don't understand from your evidence, perhaps you'll help me. You say the HVO were outnumbered by ten to one. Do you base this on research figures or is it a matter of feel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: More or less everybody knew that there were more Muslims in Central Bosnia. That's a generally-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it may even be something that's not challenged, but you've chosen to tell us it was ten to one. Can you tell us, please, tell us what the brigades were, what the units were. Can you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I don't know. But I know that the ratio was close to that, approximately that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this something that you were told on the radio, perhaps the local Busovaca radio and television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I knew that from before that that was a generally-known thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And over what general area do you say the figure was ten to one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In the area of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DG, the question was whether what you told us about the correlation of ten to one. Is it simply a manner of speaking, or did it mean that there was a major disproportion, or is it the accurate ratio that you are offering us? That was the question that you were asked. Why one to ten rather than one to nine or one to eight.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: According to -- in my estimate, according to my knowledge, all that I knew about that, I really think that the ratio was one to ten. I knew then, and I know now, that the Muslims are -- have been much more numerous than we are. I won't mention Zenica. The population of Zenica alone equals the overall number of Croats. So it may be my estimate, but I'm quite sure about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But your estimate concerns the armed troops or the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Armed forces, armed troops and the population, because the two are connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this estimate, where do you -- where did you draw your information from; from police reports, from any particular documents? Could you identify the source?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Not police reports, simply my own knowledge about the number, about the ratios of the Muslim and Croat population. And, of course, it is common knowledge that there was a large number of Muslims who fled from the Republika Srpska had come to Kacuni and other places with a Muslim majority, so it must have been that ratio, and perhaps it was even higher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on from these early days of yours in the police force, but let's just crystalise the picture, crystalise the position as at the end of January. Who was running the war, as you understood it, for the politicians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I do not really know who it was who ran the war amongst the politicians. As far as I know and understand war, the war was run by the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, how long do you think that you will take so that we know what to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very much hoping that I'll be finished by half past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So shall we work until 4.30? I hope that the interpreters will cooperate with us. Thank you very much. I see some of them nodding their heads, and that is an international sign of an affirmative answer. So we shall work until half past four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ignorance of who's running the war might work for the ordinary soldier, might even work for the fresh, ordinary policeman. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really agree with you. It wasn't such an important post. It wasn't then. It isn't now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you really telling us that you had no idea who was behind the soldiers and who was behind the military decisions? Is that really your evidence? Is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I know that wars are waged by soldiers, that they have their commanders, and they have their superiors, and so on and so forth, who is behind it all, I mean I really -- I don't know really. I mean how could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because in Busovaca, after April, things were pretty difficult, weren't they, because you were on the losing side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Busovaca was really in a plight at the time. We were fighting for survival. It was a struggle for survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You already told us how people talked about everything, about Kostroman and Kacuni and everything else. Who did they blame for getting them into this mess, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, nobody in particular. People just realised it just had befallen them, and that is how they took it. I don't know that they blamed anyone in particular. Yes, of course, Muslims who attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about Mr. Kordic, please, because you were there as a policeman by this time. He used to be based at Tisovac, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then he moved to the basement of the PTT building for a time. Why did he do that? You were there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I do not know that it moved or when it was. I know that it was in Tisovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, did you not see him in uniform, surrounded by armed men, going into the basement of the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I saw him seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you or did you not see him in uniform? It's a very small town and you're a policeman. Did you or did you not see him going into the basement of the PTT building? I must tell you this: He was seen there by at least two --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I did not, I did not see him enter the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This would be in February, Your Honour. The reference is the 3rd and 5th of February, evidence of Jennings and Foregrave relate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you saw him around Busovaca, February, March, he was in uniform and he was guarded, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember seeing him in February at all because I was ill at the time, and right now I simply can't remember seeing him in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How about March, the month before Ahmici, to which we will turn? How about March?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Both in February and in March, I was ill. I spent most of the time at home. I did not see Mr. Dario Kordic in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness DG, without mentioning the date but during that period of time, did you ever happen to see Mr. Kordic in Busovaca? Yes or no. Without pinpointing the time, could you give us yes or no, on the basis of your memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. If you mean in 1993, yes, I used to see him, but not in the former half of the year because most of the time I was ill. When I was all right and healthy, then it was between the police station and my home. I really wasn't moving around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when is it that you remember seeing him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, I did not see him often, because there were no points of convergence between us. So there was nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you see him or did you not see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Very rarely in 1993. And to communicate, I had no need to, because there was nothing to bring us together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's just pass through Ahmici. Tell us what happened there as you understood it and from what was said on the street. Would you like to do that for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, what I heard along the grapevine was that a conflict had taken place between the HVO and ABiH troops, that there were some casualties during the conflict, and it was only later that I heard that there had also been quite a number of civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who had attacked who? Just help us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't know who attacked whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there, at any time in Busovaca, a concern that the HVO had been involved in a massacre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Any people in Busovaca condemned, censured every crime committed against people, against a member of any ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. Was there at any time in Busovaca a concern that the HVO had been involved in a massacre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer that question. You mean what I heard in Busovaca, what kind of stories went round?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Witness DG, you've been asked by Mr. Kordic's counsel to give accounts about what you heard about Kostroman. I want you to tell the Judges what you heard, and in particular whether you heard on the street that the HVO had been involved in a massacre at Ahmici, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I don't think I heard anything along those lines. People condemned crimes, any crimes committed by anyone against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because isn't the truth of this matter that you may have known or had got to know Kordic was taking an increasing military role over these months, culminating in the disaster both for the dead and also for you, the Croats, because you overreached yourself at Ahmici? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I did not hear anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's move forward. Muslims in Busovaca may have been coming in as refugees, but they were being pushed out or moved out very quickly, many of them to Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, it is not correct, because I don't know that they were forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And let's deal with the crime on the streets. Present in this small town of Busovaca was the limited police force of which you were a member and the HVO military side; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Both the -- there were both civilian and military police in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Young men of military age had to join up and fight; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: They did not have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, then they must have joined it of their own wish. It was a struggle for survival. If you are faced with a situation where your parents, brothers and sisters are under threat, then of course you will go to fight. Nobody needs to call you to do that. Because when you have a wife and three children, then you fight. You simply cannot but fight. There is no other way out, and that is what happened in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And all the young men went to fight, pretty well, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I should say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who was left to do the crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I do not know who committed crimes. If I had any such knowledge, they would be prosecuted, and we did prosecute all the cases that were known to us. But you must know that combatants spent at the front line -- sometimes they would come back home. They spent a month or two in the trenches, there were refugees arriving daily or leaving, and they all wanted to get away from the area, naturally, because we did not know then that we would survive, that we would not fall. And it is difficult now, at this point of time, to say who committed crimes because we simply did not have any control over the territory. We did not know who was there; what kind of a record, where he was moving, what he was doing, what kind of weapons, what kind of equipment, explosives. You name them, the place was full to the brim with all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must suggest to you that the combined influence of the HVO military side and the police meant that control could be exercised, if you had wanted to do it, and that if there were crimes being committed, maybe they were crimes committed against Muslims. Would that be right? Was it crimes against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: The civilian police did all within its power to prevent crimes, to record them and, if nothing else, to take note of all that was going on so that sooner or later, if not then, then perhaps now, such crimes could be investigated. Under the conditions under which we had to work, and they were very difficult, I really think we did our utmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard about the man, Kristo, and we've heard evidence of his speaking of Muslims in derogatory terms, saying they should be permitted on the territory but as it were with rights -- with very limited rights. Did he talk to you in those terms about Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I did not hear that and Mr. Kristo never talked to me in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember a girl called Fatima who had to go to Zenica because she was very pregnant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many policemen were there in the police station in the summer of 1993, half a dozen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you the figure, but those who were involved in police business. There were never more than five or six of them at any given time and, of course, their number would drop down or increase depending on the need for those people at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, I wonder if you can just help the Judges with this: Kristo had to be freed to go to Zenica, and Mr. Kordic was involved in all that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now, (redacted), I've asked you once but I will ask you again: Who appointed you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I guess the municipal council. There was nobody else until the end of the conflict when the police administration, of course, could observe all the rules of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that mean Mr. Kordic appointed you or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
