utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. So may we take it that had you no special relationship with Mr. Kordic? Correct me if I am wrong, but that would seem to follow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, not any special relationship. I don't really understand what you mean, what kind of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to questions that you were asked by His Honour, Judge Bennouna, just briefly. Tell us again what category of documents did you choose to send to Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, as for those documents, they had to do with some general problems such as problems in the work of the Red Cross. People were really protesting. They were very dissatisfied, but it had to do with the food shortage, and that is something like that because I thought it was very important for a politician to know because it could give rise to some discontent. And information about the police work, about the dissatisfaction of people. If people are not satisfied with the police work, then you need to submit some information about your work so that they would understand you better to realise that things were not all that bad as they might seem; or rather to present true facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive me if I've got it wrong and, of course, wartimes are different conditions from peacetimes, but those documents might seem to have some -- the quality of confidentiality about them. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I don't really know how confidential they were because a politician could always obtain them one way or the other, and now to the municipal chief you submit reports on work and activities and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be that senior politicians could obtain documents by one means or the other if they went through the appropriate channels, but that's not what you're telling us. You're telling us you provided certain documents to Mr. Kordic of your own initiative. Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Not Mr. Kordic only, other politicians. For instance, Zoran Maric, I also submitted such information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: He was not the only one. (redacted) (redacted), of course, I wanted people to know about my work. I mean people who could affect my work in some way. I mean people who were in politics, I suppose. It's always been like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Maric was the mayor. He had a legitimate interest in being fed information from below. Please, try and help us. What was Mr. Kordic's role in your community that warranted his being sent unasked, confidential documents, if they were confidential?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that they were confidential. And as for the rest, I simply thought it might be good if I informed, among other people, Mr. Kordic, about the work and certain problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any other local figure in Busovaca who had more political power than Mr. Kordic that you can identify so that the Judges can have the name in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I do not know who was that politician or any politicians and what were their powers. But now that people who heard a name in politics where Kordic, Zoran Maric, Niko Grubesic, and what do you know -- I mean people like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you became -- are you suggesting that any of those people was superior in political power to Mr. Kordic; Mr. Grubesic, for example? Are you really suggesting that he wielded more power than Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I do not know which one of them had more political authority, more political power.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you got the job (redacted), that would have required -- well, you had no real police skills apart from six months on the job, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, yes. I did not go through any particular police training, but I knew more or less what that work meant since I had worked for an inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And tell us, did you get political push, political patronage to get that job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, at that time, it wasn't much of an office, nor was it very rewarding one. So I do not think that there was any patronage was needed for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what jobs have you been doing recently, what jobs are you doing now? You're still in the government, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you, at any stage, been in private enterprise yourself or have you always been a government employee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: A government employee all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you had --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I was for the -- with the executive branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you had any other source of income apart from your government salaries, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The mosque -- and that's my last question because of time -- the mosque, you suggested that it had been shelled, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence to that effect. Must the witnesses saying that be wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: I do not know what those witnesses said, but I could not say anything like that because there was a report about that and I wasn't there all by myself. There were firemen and lots of people around. So at that time, one could not say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was it set on fire then if it wasn't shelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: Well, must have been some perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is it really the case in your small town -- and I accept that times were difficult -- is it really the case that there was no water and no machine available to try and put out the fire or was that part of a continuing policy of oppression of the Muslims, please, to let it burn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DG
utterances.text: In 1993, in Busovaca, there was nothing, fuel, food, ammunition, and all the rest, spare parts. I mean, it is difficult to say what there was in some supplies since there was nothing. And I was really very happy with our fire brigade at that time. I know that at a later stage a vehicle arrived from Mediapan or somewhere, and I'm sure they did all they could to put the fire out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe we have now come to the end of this testimony. Witness DG, thank you for coming and giving your evidence before the Chamber of the International Tribunal. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we part company today, there is, I believe, one more witness who will be left over from your list, Mr. Sayers, the list for the next week. You thought if we would not be able to finish the witnesses who we had on the list, but then next week, according to your list, we shall have two witnesses, two of them confidential, that is, people who have applied for protective measures, if I understood well what you were asking us to do. Then we shall have four witnesses more, Mr. Zoran Delic, Arapovic, Santic, Avaric [phoen]. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's it precisely Your Honour, and I'm glad to say that we finished the witness today so there wouldn't be any carryover for the next week, he won't have to stay around on the weekend, and we remain dead on schedule to complete by the time estimate that we have given the Trial Chamber, to complete our case-in-chief, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you have already noted, there will be no sessions on Monday, and we shall resume, I hope with President May, who will, I hope, recover, on Tuesday, the 29th, at half past nine. This session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: at 4.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of May, 2000 at 9.30 a.m. 25
